title: Dhotaka's question (Sn 5)
hookLine: read it: I can't free you; know the teaching and cross yourself
tomorrow: if you have to cross alone, what do you hold onto?

cards: Midnight before the exam, and the message to the friend who gets it: please, just send me your answers. Or the call to a parent: just tell me what to do. Now the same moment, long ago.
A young man named Dhotaka has come a long way with other students to question the Buddha. He's already asked once to hear the teaching. Now he bows.
I see you, he says, a sage who owns nothing, walking the world. I bow to you. Free me from my doubts.
And the Buddha says: I can't.

teach.b: Here's the rest of that line, in Dhotaka's question. I am not able to free anyone in the world who has doubts.

teach.h: KNOW THE TEACHING, CROSS THE FLOOD.
teach.b: But when you know the best teaching, you will cross this flood yourself. It lands hard at first. The student is on his knees, and the teacher says no.
But listen to what's inside the no. The Buddha doesn't send him away. Earlier in the same exchange he's already told him: be ardent, wise and mindful, listen, and train yourself toward peace.
After the no, he keeps teaching.

He offers to describe a peace that isn't hearsay, one you can see for yourself here and now, and says: whatever you know, above, below, across, in the middle, see it as a tie to the world, and don't build craving on it.
So the no isn't a closed door. It's a map, and a refusal to carry him. Doubt, in this story, isn't something a teacher can lift off you like a coat.

That's the strange respect in the answer: the Buddha treats Dhotaka as someone able to cross. The teaching is given; the crossing is his. And the far shore in these poems is the image for that whole path.
Nobody gets ferried. Each one crosses.

how: Theravada teachers often cite Dhotaka's question alongside the saying that the Buddhas only point the way: the teaching is offered, and each person practices it themselves.

o: a ferryman who carried the Buddha's students across a river
a student who begged to be freed from doubt, and was told to cross
a teacher's riddle given to students before a long journey

p: bows: free me from my doubts
I can't free anyone who doubts
see it as a tie to the world

s: when the Buddha says he can't free Dhotaka, he sends him away
he keeps teaching: a peace seen here and now, and every known thing seen as a tie.
the Buddha tells Dhotaka he will cross the flood himself
knowing the best teaching, you will cross this flood yourself.
in Buddhism, a teacher's blessing is what removes a student's doubt
in this story, doubt clears as the student knows and walks the teaching himself.

games.q: your little brother is stuck on a hard puzzle and begs you to just solve it. what would Dhotaka's answer have you do?
o: show him how to look at it, then let him find the last move himself.
solve it for him; helping means taking the hard part away.
walk off and tell him he's on his own, since nobody can help.
games.why: the Buddha said no to carrying Dhotaka, and then kept teaching. the way is shown; the crossing is the student's own.

practice: If you can, stand up and take a few slow steps, as slow as you can manage. Feel each foot lift, move and land, and notice that no one else can take this step for you.
Then sit again and rest, feeling the floor under your feet until the bell.

wordCard.voice: Dhotaka's question: a student bows and asks to be freed from doubt. The Buddha says he can't free anyone, but whoever knows the teaching crosses the flood themselves.

orig.note: Pali: flood. The flood each student asks how to cross.

carryVoice: For the riverbank in front of you: cross yourself, with the map in hand. Day sixteen seventy-four, walked.

sources.ref: Sutta Nipata 5.6 (Dhotakamanavapuccha, Dhotaka's question, in the Parayanavagga)
